newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Wheat prices seen remaining volatile, unstable.
newsitem.headline: Wheat prices seen remaining volatile, unstable.

text.p: Wheat prices will probably remain volatile and unstable as the world tries to rebuild its stocks from recent lows, an official of U.S. Wheat Associates said on Friday.
John Howard of U.S. Wheat Associates told an Asia rice conference in Singapore that wheat prices in the spring of 1997 may remain volatile as the world rebuilds its stocks.
"Prices are volatile and unstable. We are still in the process of rebuilding stocks," he said.
World wheat ending stocks in the 1995/96 (July 1/June 30) marketing year was estimated by the Food and Agriculture Organisation to reach only 101.5 million tonnes, the smallest figure since 1980/81.

The U.S. Agriculture Department (USDA) said earlier this month, world ending stocks in 1996/97 should rise to 116.5 million tonnes, helped partly by the projected world wheat harvest in 1996/97 of 518 million tonnes, the second highest on record.
The low stocks and uncertainties over the U.S. crop drove wheat prices to a year-high of US$215 a tonne FOB Portland last May from $147 a tonne FOB in April, 1995.
The price dropped to $161 a tonne FOB recently after doubts over the U.S. wheat crop this year were dispelled.
"But still, it's wrong to be complacent," Richard Woodhams, assistant executive director of the International Grains Council (IGC) in Britain, told the conference.
"If there is not enough rain, we might see a repeat performance. We're not necessarily out of the woods yet," he said.
